{
  "winner": "B",
  "reasons": [
    "Idea A has a hard gate on the 90-day timeline. Per the brief, becoming an Authorized IRS e-file Provider can take up to 45 days, including an application, a suitability check and fingerprinting. That eats half the window before a full filer could legally transmit returns. Idea B's baseline tracker has no comparable regulatory gate.",
    "Idea B's minimum product is described as buildable in six weeks by one person with agents: deadline tracking, alerts, document storage and a dashboard. It matches published $49/mo comparables (Expiration Reminder, RenewalTracker), so a first paying customer is plausible within 90 days.",
    "An error costs more in Idea A. The brief says PFIC, FBAR and FATCA mistakes can cost customers tens of thousands of dollars, which demands trust a new solo product lacks. Idea B also carries liability, but a narrowly scoped tracker that skips rule-change monitoring can limit that exposure.",
    "Idea B's demand evidence comes from three separate occupational communities (engineers, therapists, small-business owners) describing the same recurring pain. Idea A's quotes also show real pain, but none show dissatisfaction with the existing $169-$199 investor tiers.",
    "Both markets are crowded with priced competitors, so competition does not separate them. The deciding factor is time-to-first-revenue, and Idea B's path has fewer structural blockers."
  ],
  "weakest_evidence_in_loser": "Idea A's claim that the investor/PFIC sub-segment is 'validated, underserved' rests on incumbents charging upsells for it (Expatfile Investor $199, H&R Block $169 + $99 per Form 8621). That evidence shows the segment is already served and monetized, not underserved. The brief offers no data showing these customers are dissatisfied with existing tools or would switch. The low-cost community channel it relies on also has no cost data, and the brief notes incumbents already have presence there.",
  "confidence_note": "Moderate. Idea A has stronger willingness-to-pay evidence: incumbents at 165k and 100k users. Idea B has real weaknesses: the CPL figures come from what the brief itself calls an AI-aggregated blog and are only directional, and the brief admits spreadsheet inertia may be the true competitor. The pick rests mainly on Idea A's IRS authorization delay and high error stakes versus the 90-day goal. If Idea A were narrowed to a standalone PFIC calculator that needs no e-file authorization, the comparison could flip, but neither brief tests that variant."
}
